## What Is an Employer of Record in Jamaica


An[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer of a worker in Jamaica on paper, while you stay in control of their day-to-day work, projects, and performance. The EOR signs the employment contract, runs payroll, and handles the local compliance paperwork. You decide what the person does and how they do it.


This structure exists because of a practical legal reality. If your company has no registered entity in Jamaica, you generally cannot issue a compliant Jamaican employment contract or run local payroll on your own. Jamaica’s employment framework expects an employer with a local legal presence, local tax registrations, and local payroll setup already in place. An EOR already holds those pieces, so it can step in as the legal employer while you direct the work itself.


For a US or UK company, this is the difference between hiring a Jamaican employee this month or waiting several months for entity registration, tax setup, and legal review before anyone can start. The EOR route skips that wait while keeping the hire compliant under Jamaican law.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Jamaica


Jamaica’s employment framework is anchored by the[Labour Relations and Industrial Disputes Act](https://laws.moj.gov.jm/library/subsidiary-legislation/the-labour-relations-and-industrial-disputes-act) and the Employment (Termination and Redundancy Payments) Act, which generally govern written employment contracts, notice periods, and severance pay. Employers are typically required to register workers with the[National Insurance Scheme (NIS)](https://mlss.gov.jm/departments/national-insurance-scheme/) and remit contributions to the NIS, the National Housing Trust (NHT), and education tax, in addition to standard payroll income tax withholding. Jamaican law also sets a national minimum wage and statutory entitlements such as paid vacation and sick leave, along with a probationary period that generally runs up to 90 days before full employment protections apply. Termination generally calls for written notice scaled to an employee’s length of service, and getting that calculation wrong is one of the more common ways employers run into disputes with Jamaica’s Ministry of Labour and Social Security. None of these obligations disappear when you hire through an EOR, since the EOR’s local registrations and payroll setup are what let it absorb this compliance burden on your behalf. This is general information, not legal advice, and specific obligations can vary by role, industry, and company size, so confirming details with a local expert is worth doing before finalizing an offer.

## Cost of Hiring in Jamaica with an EOR vs. a Local Entity


Setting up your own entity in Jamaica means incorporation fees, local legal and accounting support, and ongoing compliance infrastructure before you can issue a single paycheck, a process that typically stretches over several months. An EOR skips that buildout entirely: you pay a predictable per-employee cost that bundles the contract, payroll, and compliance work the EOR already has in place, with no incorporation or entity maintenance fees to carry on your books. That difference adds up. Hiring the same employee through an EOR generally costs around 70% less than setting up and maintaining your own local entity, once legal, accounting, and compliance overhead are factored in. The gap narrows as headcount grows, since entity costs are mostly fixed while EOR fees scale per employee, which is why a local entity tends to make more financial sense only once you have enough people in Jamaica to make it worth the cost. For a first hire or two, the EOR route is almost always the cheaper and faster option.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Jamaica: Which Is Right for You


Choosing between an EOR and a local entity in Jamaica usually comes down to how long you plan to stay and how many people you expect to hire there. An EOR fits best when you’re making your first few Jamaican hires, want to move quickly, and would rather not take on the legal and tax exposure of operating in a new jurisdiction. A local entity starts to make more financial sense once you have enough headcount in Jamaica that the fixed costs of incorporation, local legal support, and ongoing compliance infrastructure get spread across more employees than the per-employee EOR fee would cost. There’s also a control trade-off: a local entity gives you more flexibility on equity structuring and direct IP ownership, while an EOR gets you compliant and paying someone in days instead of months. For most companies hiring their first person in Jamaica, the EOR route is the faster, lower-risk starting point, with a local entity becoming the better long-term option only after the team there grows.
